title: Chapter XXIV

teacherSummary.text: Caroline's letter confirms the Bingleys will stay in London. Jane bears it quietly. Elizabeth reflects bitterly on the 'inconsistency of all human characters.' Mr. Bennet jokes that Wickham would make a fine jilt.

vocabulary.definition: To renounce all claim to deny
vocabulary.context: Miss Bennet eagerly disclaimed all extraordinary merit, and threw back the praise on her sister’s warm affection.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disclaim”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Miss Bennet was the only creature who could suppose there might be any extenuating circumstances in the case, unknown to the society of Hertfordshire; her mild and steady candour always pleaded for allowances, and urged the possibility of mistakes—but by everybody else Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “extenuate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + ten (Latin tenere, "to hold") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: They saw him often, and to his other recommendations was now added that of general unreserve.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unreserve”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To enter by gradual steps or by stealth into the possessions or rights of another
vocabulary.context: Do not be afraid of my running into any excess, of my encroaching on your privilege of universal good will.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “encroach”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The more I see of the world, the more am I dissatisfied with it; and every day confirms my belief of the inconsistency of all human characters, and of the little dependence that can be placed on the appearance of either merit or sense.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “confirm”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Her many attractions were again dwelt on, and Caroline boasted joyfully of their increasing intimacy, and ventured to predict the accomplishment of the wishes which had been unfolded in her former letter.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “predict”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + dict (Latin dicere, "to say"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Wickham’s society was of material service in dispelling the gloom, which the late perverse occurrences had thrown on many of the Longbourn family.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “occurrence”: cur (Latin cura, "care") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of conjoining, or the state of being conjoined, united, or associated
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conjunction”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: But if I go on, I shall displease you by saying what I think of persons you esteem.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “displease”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The state or quality of being entire or complete
vocabulary.context: You shall not, for the sake of one individual, change the meaning of principle and integrity, nor endeavour to persuade yourself or me, that selfishness is prudence, and insensibility of danger, security for happiness.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “integrity”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Women's feelings were expected to be hidden for propriety.

significance: Elizabeth's cynicism shows how disappointment shapes judgment.
discussionQuestions: How does Jane's restraint compare with Elizabeth's response?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIV,” how does Austen show disappointment and philosophy? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIV develops the idea of disappointment and philosophy. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXIV to complicate the reader's understanding of disappointment and philosophy. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of disappointment and philosophy responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of disappointment and philosophy. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: The act of conjoining, or the state of being conjoined, united, or associated

satQuestions.passage: Hope was over, entirely over; and when Jane could attend to the rest of the letter, she found little, except the professed affection of the writer, that could give her any comfort. Miss Darcy’s praise occupied the chief of it. Her many attractions were again dwelt on, and Caroline boasted joyfully of their increasing intimacy, and ventured to predict the accomplishment of the wishes which had been unfolded in her former letter. She wrote also with great pleasure of her brother’s being an inmate of Mr. Darcy’s house, and mentioned with raptures, some plans of the latter with regard to new furniture.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXIV”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does Jane's restraint compare with Elizabeth's response? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are disclaimed, extenuating, unreserve, encroaching, confirms. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Miss Bennet eagerly disclaimed all extraordinary merit, and threw back the praise on her sister’s warm affection.” Webster's says: To renounce all claim to deny. Now the word history: “disclaim”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “extenuate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + ten (Latin tenere, "to hold") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “unreserve”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Women's feelings were expected to be hidden for propriety. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's cynicism shows how disappointment shapes judgment. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to disappointment and philosophy.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXIV,” how does Austen show disappointment and philosophy? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about disappointment and philosophy, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes disappointment and philosophy. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
